title: Prosecution of Deepfake Crimes: How Indian Courts Are Building a Doctrine without a Statute
author: Anjaneya Pai
excerpt: Prosecution of Deepfake Crimes: How Indian Courts Are Building a Doctrine without a Statute
content:
"We may take judicial notice of the fact that we are living in the era of deepfakes” was the acknowledgement of the Delhi High Court in the case of Nirmaan Malhotra v. Tushita Kaul[1], wherein a husband presented images alleging his wife’s adultery to the Court, in the course of challenging a maintenance order passed by the Court.

It has been observed that such issues have confronted Indian Courts since 2023, as evidenced by Anil Kapoor v. Simply Life India & Ors., wherein the Delhi High Court granted an injunction restraining sixteen entities and, notably, the world at large, from utilising the veteran Bollywood actor's name, likeness, image, or AI/face-morphing/GIF tools for commercial or financial gain without obtaining his consent. This case — the foremost judgment adjudicating an AI-generated deepfake — is said to reflect a disparity in accessibility to litigation: content of a commercial nature is more easily taken down than sexualised deepfake content, as observed by Tech Law Forum, run by the students of NALSAR University of Law, Hyderabad[2].

Deepfake crime may be said to range across identity theft, financial fraud, electoral disinformation, non-consensual intimate imagery, and defamation, each testing statutes that remain unequipped to adjudicate such conduct, since existing legislation was not designed to assess AI-generated harm. With a layering of old criminal provisions, freshly notified intermediary rules, and a judiciary willing to stretch constitutional doctrine to fill gaps that Parliament has been slower to close, deepfake crimes in India are adjudicated.

In Light of the Statute

Section 66[3] of the Information Technology Act[4] is broad enough to accommodate penalization of certain dimensions of cyber related offences; it may be understood as the handle of an umbrella with distinct canopies,

1.         Section 66A[5] penalises offensive messages transmitted through communication services;
2.         Section 66B[6] punishes the dishonest receipt of stolen computer resource or communication devices;
3.         Section 66C[7] deals with the protection of personality rights and proscribes identity theft;
4.         Section 66D[8] covers cheating by personation through the medium of a computer resource; and
5.         Section 66E[9] addresses the publishing of private images, in contravention of the Right to Privacy enshrined under Article 21[10], by virtue of Puttaswamy J[11].

A purposive reading of these provisions, rather than adherence to their bare letter, has extended their reach considerably. The provision relating to identity theft has been interpreted to cover the non-consensual use of a person's unique identification features, including but not limited to facial geometry and voice biometrics. This interpretive leap has widened a provision originally drafted for phishing and impersonation, extending it to accommodate the replication of human likeness.

The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023[12], adds further, covering the ambit of identity theft under Section 319[13], coupled with criminal intimidation and defamation, while the Protection of Women from Cybercrime provisions under the BNS offer certain remedies for sexually explicit deepfakes.

What emerges is not a code but a mirage of code, with borrowed provisions and stretched interpretation, which renders the delivery of justice dependent on two factors: the capability of the lawyer arguing the matter, and the willingness of the honourable Judge to weave the criminal act into the soul of the section.

The IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules, notified on 10 February 2026, are India's first legislative effort to curb deepfakes and harmful AI-generated content, introducing "Synthetically Generated Information." Rule 2(1)(wa) defines synthetically generated information as audio, visual or audio-visual information, artificially or algorithmically created, generated, modified or altered using a computer resource, in a manner that such information purports to appear real, authentic or true and depicts or portrays any individual or event in a manner that is, or is likely to be perceived as indistinguishable from a natural person or real-world event.

Significant Social Media Intermediaries are mandated to comply to label AI-generated content with watermark inserted onto the image or video surface. Takedowns of harmful AI-generated or deepfake content within three hours of receiving a complaint or government notification, failing which they risk losing safe harbour protection guaranteed under Section 79 of the IT Act[14].

The 2026 Amendment Rules also condition safe harbour protection under Section 79 on compliance: platforms that knowingly facilitate synthetically generated information in contravention of any statute, or that fail to exercise due diligence by deploying the required detection tools, forfeit that protection.

Lately, a horde of actors including Nandamuri Taraka Rama Rao Jr., R. Madhavan, and Shilpa Shetty secured court orders blocking the dissemination of deepfake videos. This, de facto, indicates that a right to digital personality may be justiciable.

In Sadhguru Jagadish Vasudev & Anr. v. Igor Isakov & Ors., the Delhi High Court introduced and granted an order extending protection against repeated infringement to new mirror and rogue websites, without requiring a suit to be filed. Courts have thus combined personality-rights protection with copyright and trademark doctrine.

Content whose authenticity is questioned must still comply with certification under Section 65B of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023. A certificate obtained under Section 65B authenticates that a recording was produced by a functioning device, without taking into account whether the content of that recording is a product of unethical manufacturing or doctoring. It has become common practice in Indian trial courts for evidence to be challenged even after due certification, with defence counsel alleging during cross-examination that a recording is an AI fabrication. In the absence of a statutory threshold, benchmarks, or guidelines for forensic examination, each case must be assessed individually on the reliability of its evidence.

Conclusion
Every legal system eventually meets its limitations, stumbling across a technology that it remains unequipped to handle. Let the facts be clear: four cases were adjudicated in 2024, and nineteen in 2025, numbers disproportional to the incidence of deepfake crimes committed across the country. This reflects an imbalance in the delivery of justice, which leaves the adjudication of deepfake crimes to proceed on a case-by-case, injunction-by-injunction basis. Though the resourcefulness of the Courts — which decline to take the legitimacy of a photograph at face value — must be lauded, improvisation, however skilful it may be, can never be equated to legislative security. Such cases are decided on three factors: the capability of the lawyer to articulate the facts, the unorthodox interpretation of the statute by the Judge, and lastly, perhaps, the privilege of the litigant to possess the resources to litigate it. Ending on an honest note, this makes it one of the more interesting moments to be practising law in the country.

title: Stateless by Design
author: Sanskrati Jain
excerpt: Can a child be denied a nationality because of their parents' immigration status? This article examines the gaps in India's citizenship framework and explores the legal reforms needed to prevent statelessness.
content:
Children must not suffer for their parents’ lack of documentation. Unfortunately, this is the case in India. A child born in India is protected by neither the Citizenship Act, 1955 (“Act”) nor by certain international frameworks such as Convention on the Rights of the Child (“CRC”). This is not merely a consequence of a gap in implementation; rather, it reflects the legal position under Indian law. However, this does not apply to every child born in India. It specifically affects children born to an "illegal migrant," as defined under the Act.

What Does the Law Say?

Since 2003, Section 3(1)(c) of the Citizenship Act, 1955 demands that a child born in India must be born to parents that are both Indian citizens or one that is an Indian citizen and other that is not an “illegal migrant”.  Additionally, a proviso inserted in Section 2(1)(b) of the Act through an amendment in 2019 categorically excludes children of Muslim migrants from obtaining citizenship.  An “illegal migrant” as defined in Section 2(1)(b) of the Act is a person that has either entered the country without authorised documents such as a valid passport or with valid documents but continues to reside beyond permitted duration.  
In situations where citizenship is in question, it becomes important to consult not only domestic but also international legal standards. Indian law treats citizenship as a right to be inherited and not an immediate entitlement upon birth.  Article 7 of the CRC, on the other hand explicitly accords a child with the right to a nationality immediately upon birth.  The same provision ensures that a child remains protected, stating that parties to the convention must abide by and effectively implement the obligations to the convention particularly when a child may be rendered stateless due to discrepancies in domestic law. India accepted the obligation of the right to a nationality in 1992 but did not ratify a specific enforcement or redressal system for the same. The 1954 Convention relating to the Status of Stateless Persons seeks to ensure non-discrimination on grounds of race, religion or country of origin.  The 1961 Convention on Reduction of Statelessness obligates parties to create protections to prevent statelessness at birth and later in life and providing nationality to children born in countries where they would otherwise be rendered stateless.

The CRC together with the 1954 and 1961 conventions would provide for a seamless protection and redressal system for children born in India that could be rendered stateless due to domestic law. However, India is not a party to either the 1954 Convention or the 1961 Convention. This creates a legal vacuum for children born in such unfortunate circumstances, wherein each legal framework is internally coherent and defensible on its own terms and so, children who fall within this gap are left without effective protection. The issue is that for a child born in India to a parent that is an “illegal migrant” there is no single institution that can be individually held responsible, and this creates a harder battle for the child to defend his or her right to acquire a nationality.

The most practical solution lies within the Act itself. Section 5 already permits citizenship by registration for specific categories of persons, including minor children of Indian citizens,  and this same mechanism could be extended to children who would otherwise be rendered stateless under Section 3(1)(c) . This does not require inventing a new legislative framework, only widening an existing one to a population currently excluded from it. Complete ratification of the 1961 Convention, with its broad obligation to grant nationality in most circumstances, may not be a step India is prepared to take, particularly for a country managing a population of 1.4 billion, but a registration pathway carries none of that structural risk and addresses the same issue at its root. Ratifying the 1954 Convention would remain a useful complementary step, ensuring that children who fall through the cracks are at least treated with dignity and free from discrimination, but it cannot substitute for a domestic mechanism that prevents statelessness at birth in the first place.

Ultimately, this issue extends beyond inconsistencies in the law. It concerns identity, belonging, dignity, and legal security for children. No child should have to go through battles of nationality throughout their childhood and later adulthood, protections must exist and if they fail, clearly established redressal systems must be there to secure the child.
